newsitem.title: USA: Chevron sees likely exit of Point Arguello.
newsitem.headline: Chevron sees likely exit of Point Arguello.

text.p: Chevron Corp is likely to cease production at its Point Arguello field offshore central California between 1999 and 2001, unless the poor economics of the field change, a Chevron spokeswoman said on Monday.

"We're looking at where the end of the project might be, and based on the information we have right now 1999 to 2001 is the window within which we see production ending." said Chevron spokeswoman Diana Vavrek.
She said lower-than-forecast oil prices and field output since the project was designed, have prevented Chevron from realizing the profits it had projected.

However, Vavrek stressed the company has not yet begun the process of shutting in production, and could still reverse its plans if oil prices rise substantially or of another party shows interest in acquiring the field.
In fact, at the same time it was forecasting an early exit from the field, Chevon was also taking steps to extend the field's life as long as possible.

Last Friday, Chevron said it and the other producers of Point Arguello received approval "to unitize the field", a move that would lower operating costs by making Chevron the operator for all the other producers.
Chevron has a stake of about 26 percent in Point Arguello, which is located off the coast of Santa Barbara. Phillips Petroleum Co and Texaco Inc are the other major partners.

Texaco was not immediately available for comment, but a spokesman for Phillips said that company would cease production whenever Chevron chose to do so. He said Phillips took a $45 million charge in the first quarter related to Point Arguello. In a quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Chevron also said it may take a writedown to shut in the field, but did not specify an amount.

If Point Arguello were to be shut by the year 2001, it would mean a producing life of just 10 years for a field that had once been considered one of the most promising oil finds in the U.S., expected to produce for at least 25 years.
But since the field was discovered in 1981, it has been dogged by a series of mishaps, beginning with environmentalists' objections that delayed production by 10 years.

The strict drilling and tankering procedures Chevron finally agreed to substantially hiked up operating costs when production began in 1991. Those problems were compounded by a sharp drop in world oil prices and the discovery that the oil from Point Arguello was some of the poorest quality in the U.S. Today, Point Arguello crude fetches only about $14.50 a barrel, compared with about $21.70 for crude from Alaska and $24.50 for some Texas grades. Its viscous quality also makes it more expensive than other grades to produce.

"The projections for (Point Arguello) did not materialize," said Chevron's Vavrek. "We had anticipated a higher price for a barrel of oil than we are currently getting, and the reservoir has not produced as we had originally anticipated."
